narratives.narrative: Sense (101): the psalmist is 'languishing', his bones troubled (Psa 6:2). Type (102) is a state, not an act the self performs but a condition it is in. Source (103) is absent — no cause is named at the word itself; the surrounding verses hint at God's rebuke, but the languishing is reported bare, as sheer weakness. Seat (104) is explicitly 'none': this collapse is not lodged in one organ but suffered by the whole person — though the discovery (114) notes it reaches the bones, so the interior distress registers as bodily give-way. Bearer (105) is the psalmist himself; operation (106) is that the self is languishing, its very frame shaken — weakness carried down into the skeleton. Target (107) is his own frailty: the process turns inward, the self undone by its own giving-out. Manner (108) is 'none' — no how is specified; intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are all absent, so the reading stops at the state and does not track a degree or an outcome. Coupling (112) binds the languishing to itself as the marking condition. Prohibition (113) is absent — nothing is forbidden or commanded. Role (115) is a characteristic; locus (116) is internal, an inner-being state. The whole picture is of an inner-being process of depletion so deep it is felt in the bones, laid before God without any named cause.
narratives.story: The psalmist says he is wasting away, and the trouble has gone right down into his bones. It is not something he is doing but a state he has sunk into — a weakness that shakes his whole frame. We are not told what caused it, and it isn't pinned to any single part of him; it simply overtakes the whole person and is felt in the body. Nothing is said about how severe it grows or where it leads — the moment holds only the collapse itself, carried inward and laid open before God.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): 'weary with my moaning' (Psa 6:6). Type (102) a state. Source (103) is absent as a formal slot, yet the discovery (114) is precise: the weariness is depletion — the sustained groaning has drained the interior of strength; the moaning is the wearing agent named within the operation, not as an outside cause. Seat (104) is 'none': the exhaustion is not organ-located but wears down the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist; operation (106) is that the self is worn out by its own groaning — grief exhausting the whole person, a process where the very expression of sorrow consumes the one expressing it. Target (107) is exhaustion itself. Manner (108) is 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) all absent — no degree, no qualifier, no tracked outcome; the reading rests on the depletion. Coupling (112) is weary-to-moaning: the fatigue is welded to the night-long weeping the passage describes. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. An inner-being process in which sorrow, endlessly voiced, empties the self of strength.
narratives.story: He is worn out by his own groaning. Night after night his weeping has drained him until there is no strength left — the very act of grieving has used him up. It is not fixed in any one part of him; the tiredness soaks through the whole person. We aren't told how far it goes or what comes of it; the point is simply that sorrow, poured out without end, has emptied him.
narratives.variation_note: This weariness differs from the same word at Psa 69:3. Here at 6:6 the wearing agent is the psalmist's own inward moaning — grief that exhausts from within — whereas at 69:3 the same weariness comes specifically from crying out to God and waiting unanswered. Both lack a bodily seat, but the source differs: self-consuming sorrow here, unrewarded petition there.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): 'see my affliction' (Psa 9:13). Type (102) a state. Source (103) is absent — no external agent of the affliction is fixed at the word, though the verse frames it as coming 'from those who hate me'. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located, borne by the whole self. Bearer (105) is the psalmist; operation (106) is that the self pleads its own affliction from those who hate it, asking to be lifted from the gates of death. Target (107) is personal-suffering — the particular, individual misery, distinguished (discovery 114) from the general 'afflicted' class the psalm elsewhere names: here the self brings its own case, poised between death's gates and rescue. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent — no degree or outcome tracked; the reading holds the plea itself. Coupling (112) is 'my-affliction' — the suffering owned as the speaker's own. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. The inner-being movement is a suffering self turning its particular anguish Godward as the ground of its appeal for grace.
narratives.story: The psalmist asks God to look at his own suffering — the pain that comes from people who hate him. He is not speaking of others' troubles here but bringing his own case, caught between death's door and rescue. We aren't told exactly who or what is behind it, and it isn't tied to any part of his body; it is simply his whole self in distress. He holds this misery up to God and makes it the reason God should be gracious to him.
narratives.variation_note: This affliction differs from the word's other readings. At 9:13 it is an individual's own suffering, personally owned and pleaded to God (bearer = the psalmist), unlike 44:24 where a whole nation's affliction lies unrelieved while God hides his face, 107:10 where prisoners sit in it as a plight, and 119:50 where it becomes the arena in which God's promise sustains. Here the distinctive is the single self, poised between death and deliverance.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): 'lonely and afflicted, be gracious' (Psa 25:16). Type (102) a state. Source (103) absent — no cause named at the word. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the isolation is felt by the whole self. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) the self asks God to turn and be gracious, for it is lonely and afflicted — the ache of isolation carried to God. Target (107) is loneliness: notably the affliction here is bound to solitude, an inner condition of being alone. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent — no degree or downstream result recorded; the reading rests on the named condition. Coupling (112) is 'lonely-afflicted' — solitude welded to affliction, the two naming one inner state (discovery 114). Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. The inner-being process is a self, alone and afflicted, laying that specific solitude before God for mercy.
narratives.story: The psalmist calls himself lonely and afflicted and asks God to turn toward him and be kind. What marks this suffering is its loneliness — the pain of being alone joined to the pain of affliction. No cause is named, and it isn't located in any part of the body; it is the whole self in an isolated ache. He takes that exact condition and lays it before God, asking for mercy.
narratives.variation_note: This reading differs from the item's others by its target: loneliness. At 25:16 the affliction is fused to solitude — the ache of being alone — whereas at 69:29 it is affliction-with-pain met by God's salvation, at 82:3 the class of 'the afflicted' poor wronged by unjust judges, at 88:15 a lifetime's affliction from youth, and at 102:1 the affliction from which a whole prayer rises. Here the distinctive is isolation.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): 'you hid your face; I was dismayed' (Psa 30:7). Type (102) a state. Source (103) absent as a slot, but the operation (106) makes the trigger plain: when God hid his face, the self was dismayed — the collapse of a false security once favour was withdrawn. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the terror seizes the whole self. Bearer (105) the psalmist; target (107) is dismay itself — the reading turns on the interior falling apart. The discovery (114) sharpens it: this is the terror that exposed his complacency ('I shall never be moved') — the moment God withdrew, the interior fell apart. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent — no degree or outcome tracked. Coupling (112) 'hidden-face-dismay' binds the dismay to God's hidden face as its hinge. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. The inner-being movement: presumed stability shatters into terror the instant its felt ground (God's favour) is removed.
narratives.story: The psalmist had felt secure — sure he would never be shaken. Then God hid his face, and in an instant that confidence collapsed into terror. The dread isn't lodged in one part of him; it grips his whole self. What the moment reveals is how thin his security had been: the very second the felt ground of God's favour was taken away, everything inside him fell apart.
narratives.variation_note: This dismay differs from the item's others by its bearer and trigger. At 30:7 it strikes the psalmist himself — his complacency shattering when God hides his face — whereas at 83:17 the same dread is invoked on the enemies under judgment, and at 90:7 it falls on all mortals before God's wrath. The bearer shifts from the believing self, to foes, to humankind at large — the terror is the same, its subject is not.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): 'I afflicted myself when they were sick' (Psa 35:13). Type (102) here is 'affect' — distinctively not the passive 'status/state' of the other afflict readings, but self-directed feeling-action. Source (103) absent. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) is that when his enemies were sick, the self wore sackcloth, afflicted itself with fasting, and prayed with head bowed — costly compassion once shown to those who now repay evil. Target (107) is compassion-for-enemies: the affliction is self-imposed love spent on others. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'afflict-self-for-them' welds the self-affliction to intercession for the persecutors. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): love spent on the very ones who now betray. The inner-being process is remarkable — affliction not received but self-chosen, the interior humbling itself in grief and prayer on behalf of enemies.
narratives.story: When the very people who now attack him were sick, the psalmist grieved for them: he put on sackcloth, went without food, and prayed with his head bowed low, as if mourning a brother. This is affliction he took on himself — not suffering done to him, but a costly love poured out for others. It isn't tied to any one part of him; his whole self bent down in compassion. The sharp point is that he spent this care on the same people who later betrayed him.
narratives.variation_note: This reading is the item's outlier by agent and type: here affliction is self-imposed (type 'affect') — the psalmist afflicting himself in compassion for others — whereas at 94:5 the wicked inflict affliction on God's people, and at 116:10, 119:67 and 119:107 the psalmist receives/bears affliction. Same root, but the doer shifts from the self-in-love, to the wicked-as-aggressor, to the self-as-sufferer — the difference is the finding.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): affliction (oni, 'our affliction', Psa 44:24). Type (102) is 'status' — a standing condition. This reading is distinctive because its process-slots are deliberately empty: operation (106) is 'none', target (107) is 'none', coupling (112) is 'none' — the affliction is presented not as a movement with a direction but as a bare, unrelieved status. Crucially, source (103) IS present here (unlike most in this family): the affliction is 'unrelieved while God hides his face and forgets' (v24) — the cause of its persistence is God's seeming inattention. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the nation, not an individual — a corporate sufferer. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the anguished 'why?' of the faithful sufferer — misery God seems to ignore. The inner-being reading is a whole people's affliction held as an open, unanswered condition, its persistence pinned on God's hidden face.
narratives.story: A whole people cries out over their affliction and asks why God forgets it and hides his face. Here the suffering is not described as moving anywhere or doing anything — it simply sits, unrelieved. What keeps it going, the psalm says, is that God seems to look away. It isn't the pain of one person but of a nation, and it isn't fixed in any part of the body; it is a standing misery held up in the anguished question, 'Why do you forget us?'
narratives.variation_note: This affliction stands apart from the item's others in two ways. Its bearer is the nation (corporate), not an individual as at 9:13, 107:10 and 119:50; and its process-slots are empty — no operation, target or coupling — so it reads as a bare, static status rather than a movement. It is also the one reading where a source is named: the affliction stays unrelieved because God hides his face and forgets.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be terrified / in panic (bahal, Psa 48:5) — the kings, seeing Zion, are thrown into panic. Type (102) is 'action', framing the panic as something that seizes and moves them. Source (103) absent as a slot, though the passage supplies the trigger (the sight of God's city). Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; panic grips the whole self. Bearer (105) is the kings — not the psalmist but the hostile enemy: this family reads the descent as fully as the ascent. Operation (106) is to be in panic; target (107) is 'none' — the panic is not aimed, it simply overtakes. Manner (108) is present: 'they took to flight' — the panic expresses itself in headlong flight. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) is a pair: panic is welded to being astounded — amazement tipping into terror. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the terror that routs the kings, driving them to flee the impregnable city. The inner-being process: astonishment collapsing into a panic that empties the will and forces flight.
narratives.story: The enemy kings come up against God's city, and the sight of it throws them into panic. Their amazement turns instantly to terror, and the terror shows itself in one thing: they run. The dread isn't lodged in any part of them; it seizes the whole person and empties their nerve. It isn't aimed at anything — it simply overtakes them and routs them into flight.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): anguish / writhing pain (chil, Psa 48:6). Type (102) 'status' — a condition the kings are in. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the writhing takes the whole self. Bearer (105) is the kings — again the hostile enemy, their interior collapse read at full weight. Operation (106) is 'none': like a status, no movement-verb is attached; the anguish simply holds them. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) is present and vivid: 'as of a woman in labour' — the anguish imaged as birth-pangs, convulsive and involuntary. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the anguish with trembling — the two naming one seizure of dread. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): writhing distress imaged as birth-pangs, the extremity of the terrified kings' inner collapse before God's city. The inner-being reading: dread at its extremity, a convulsive interior agony pictured as labour.
narratives.story: As the enemy kings flee God's city, an anguish grips them like the pains of a woman in labour — convulsive, unstoppable, taking over the whole body. It comes with trembling, the two together naming one seizure of terror. Nothing is said of it moving toward anything or leading anywhere; it simply holds them at the far edge of dread. It is the picture of an inner collapse so total it can only be compared to birth-pangs.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be in anguish / writhe (chul, 'my heart is in anguish', Psa 55:4). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot, though the passage traces it to the enemy's noise and the wicked's oppression. Seat (104) is present and specific here: the heart — unlike most in this family, the anguish is organ-located, lodged in the heart. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to writhe / be in anguish; target (107) 'none' — the writhing is not aimed. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the heart's anguish with 'the terrors of death fallen upon him' — the writhing welded to a dread of death. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) is internal:heart — the reading fixes the process inside the heart. Discovery (114): chul, to twist/writhe as in birth-pangs, the acute torment of the inner self, a physical figure for a soul in agony. The inner-being process: the heart convulsing under a dread of death, torment given the shape of writhing.
narratives.story: The psalmist says his heart is writhing inside him — twisting in pain like a body in agony. This one is located right in the heart, and it comes together with a terror of death that has fallen over him. It isn't aimed at anything and we aren't told where it leads; it is simply the inner self convulsing. The word pictures a soul so tormented it can only be described as twisting in pain.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): horror / shuddering (pallatsuth, 'horror overwhelms me', Psa 55:5). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the horror engulfs the whole self. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) is to overwhelm / cover him — the horror acts on the self like an engulfing flood. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) is present: 'overwhelming, covering' — the horror comes as a submerging flood. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) marks it as the climax of the dread-triad — fear and trembling culminating in horror. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the shuddering that engulfs him wholly, terror that submerges the self and drives the longing to flee. The inner-being process: dread reaching its peak, covering the whole interior like water and provoking the wish to escape.
narratives.story: Fear, then trembling, and finally a shuddering horror rolls over the psalmist and covers him completely, like being pulled under water. This is the peak of his dread — the last and worst of it. It isn't fixed in any one part of him; it submerges the whole self. Under it he can only long to get away, to fly off and be at rest.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be faint / overwhelmed (ataph, 'my heart is faint', Psa 61:2). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) is present: the heart — the fainting is organ-located in the heart. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to faint / be overwhelmed — the inner self sinking. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) is a pair binding the fainting to the heart it marks. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the swooning weakness of the overwhelmed soul; ataph, to be feeble/enveloped, the sinking of the inner self — an honest admission of exhaustion that turns to God's higher strength ('lead me to the rock that is higher than I'). The inner-being process: the heart sinking under its own weakness, and from that low point reaching for a strength above itself.
narratives.story: From the far edge of the earth the psalmist calls out with his heart failing inside him. It is a swoon of the inner self, a sinking felt right in the heart. He doesn't hide it or dress it up — he admits he is spent. And from that low, honest place he reaches upward, asking to be led to a rock higher than himself, to a strength beyond his own.
narratives.variation_note: This fainting differs from the item's others in seat and source. At 61:2 it is lodged in the heart and turns toward God's higher strength, whereas at 77:3 it sinks the spirit under grief's burden, at 102:1 it has no bodily seat and pours out as complaint under affliction, and at 107:5 it drains the wanderers' soul from hunger and thirst. Here the seat is the heart and the movement bends from weakness toward rescue.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): faint / long (kamah, 'my flesh faints for you', Psa 63:1). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) is present: the flesh — uniquely here the fainting is seated in the body, the flesh itself. Bearer (105) is the psalmist, specifically his flesh (a pair binding self and body). Operation (106) is to faint / long for; target (107) is God — and this is the key distinctive: the fainting is not collapse under distress but a longing so intense it exhausts the body, aimed at God. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the flesh's fainting with the soul's thirst — soul and flesh together pining. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) is external:god — the process reaches outward toward God as its object. Discovery (114): the longing that reaches even the body; kamah here the whole person, soul and flesh, pining for God — desire so total it exhausts the frame. The inner-being process: yearning of the entire self, soul and body, spent in reaching for God.
narratives.story: In a dry, waterless land the psalmist says his very body faints for God — not from despair, but from longing. His soul thirsts and his flesh grows weak with wanting, soul and body together pining for God like a parched land aching for water. Here the fainting is felt in the body itself, and it points entirely toward God. It is desire so complete that it wears out the whole person.
narratives.variation_note: This fainting is the family's outlier in direction and locus. Unlike the collapses of distress elsewhere, at 63:1 the fainting is a longing for God (locus external:god) — the whole self, soul and flesh, exhausted by desire rather than by suffering. The weakness is real, but it is the weakness of yearning, aimed outward at God, not the sinking of despair.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be weary / faint (yaga, 'weary with my crying out', Psa 69:3). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot, but the operation and manner name it: the weariness comes from crying out. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to grow weary. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) is present: 'with crying out, throat parched' — the fatigue expressed in a voice worn hoarse. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the weariness with the crying and the waiting for God — the wear is bound to unanswered prayer, eyes failing as they wait. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): exhaustion from unanswered prayer; yaga here the fatigue of a soul that has cried until it can cry no more. The inner-being process: petition prolonged past endurance, the self worn out by crying and watching for a God who has not yet answered.
narratives.story: The psalmist has cried out to God for so long that he is worn out — his throat is dry and his eyes are failing as he keeps watching for help that hasn't come. The weariness is the exhaustion of unanswered prayer: he has cried until he can barely cry anymore. It isn't fixed in one part of him; the whole self is spent. What wears him down is the waiting — looking and looking for a God who has not yet replied.
narratives.variation_note: This weariness differs from the same word at Psa 6:6. There the wear comes from the psalmist's own inward moaning; here at 69:3 it comes from crying out to God and waiting unanswered, throat parched and eyes failing. Both lack a bodily seat, but the source shifts from self-consuming grief to the fatigue of prayer that goes unmet.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be in despair / be sick (anash, 'I am in despair', Psa 69:20). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot, but the operation ties it to a cause: reproaches have broken his heart. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located as a slot, though the coupling links it to the broken heart. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be in despair / desperately sick — the sickness of a heart with no hope left. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the despair with the state of the broken heart — reproach shattering the heart, and despair its result. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): anash, the desperate, incurable grief that follows the broken heart — the nadir of the psalm, before the turn to praise; he looked for pity and comforters and found none. The inner-being process: reproach breaking the heart, and from that break a hopeless, sickening despair — the lowest point, with no human comfort in sight.
narratives.story: Insults and reproaches have broken the psalmist's heart, and out of that break comes a despair like a sickness with no cure. He looked for someone to pity him and for someone to comfort him, and found no one. This is the lowest point of the whole prayer — a heart shattered and a hope gone completely dark. Nothing here softens it; he simply names the bottom before, later, he can turn back to praise.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): pain (keeb, 'and in pain', Psa 69:29). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the pain belongs to the whole wounded self. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be in pain. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the pain with the affliction — 'afflicted and in pain', the two naming one wounded condition. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the suffering that accompanies the affliction; keeb here the pain of the wounded soul, from which God's salvation is asked to lift him high. The inner-being process: raw hurt joined to affliction, held up to God with the plea that his salvation set the sufferer on high.
narratives.story: The psalmist says he is afflicted and in pain — the plain hurt of a wounded self, sitting right alongside his affliction. It isn't tied to any one part of him; it is the whole person aching. He doesn't dwell on how bad it is or where it leads; he simply names the pain and asks that God's rescue lift him up out of it, high and safe.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): afflicted / poor (ani, 'but I am afflicted and in pain', Psa 69:29). Type (102) 'status'. Here source (103) IS present (unlike most afflict readings): the afflicted one is 'whom God's salvation sets on high' (v29) — the reading names the hoped-for rescue as the counter to the low estate. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be afflicted. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) is present as a pair: 'in pain' — the affliction welded to bodily pain. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the affliction with his pain, met by God's salvation. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the low estate that pleads for God's rescue; ani here the poor, afflicted psalmist whose only hope is that God's salvation will lift him from the depths — the turn from lament toward trust. The inner-being process: a self at its lowest, affliction and pain together, pivoting from complaint toward hope in God's lifting.
narratives.story: The psalmist calls himself afflicted and in pain — poor and low, hurting in body and self. But this time the low estate turns toward hope: he asks God's rescue to set him on high, and names that rescue as the very thing that answers his affliction. It is the moment the prayer begins to pivot from lament toward trust. He is at the bottom, yet already looking to be lifted.
narratives.variation_note: This afflict reading is marked by the presence of a source/counter that most others lack: God's salvation that sets him on high. Unlike the lonely affliction of 25:16, the class of the poor at 82:3, the lifelong affliction of 88:15, or the prayer-from-affliction of 102:1, here at 69:29 the affliction is paired with pain and, distinctively, hinged to the hoped-for lifting — the turn from lament toward trust.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): faint / grow feeble (ataph, 'my spirit faints', Psa 77:3). Type (102) is 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, but manner names the cause. Seat (104) is present: the spirit (ruach) — the fainting is organ-located in the spirit. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to faint / be overwhelmed. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) present: 'under the burden of grief' — the fainting comes as grief's weight crushing down. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the fainting with the spirit it overwhelms. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the swooning collapse of the inner self; ataph the feebleness that overtakes the spirit, the point where grief exhausts the very capacity to bear it — and strikingly, this faints even as the psalmist remembers God ('when I remember God, I moan'). The inner-being process: memory of God itself provoking grief, until the spirit sinks under a weight it can no longer carry.
narratives.story: When the psalmist thinks of God, he groans; and as he broods, his spirit sinks and gives way. The fainting is lodged deep in his spirit, and what crushes it is the sheer weight of grief. Remarkably, it is remembering God that brings the collapse — the thought that should comfort instead overwhelms him. His inner self simply reaches the point where it can no longer hold the weight it is carrying.
narratives.variation_note: This fainting differs from the item's others by seat and cause. At 77:3 it is lodged in the spirit (ruach) and brought on by grief's burden — provoked, strikingly, by remembering God — whereas at 61:2 it sinks the heart and turns toward rescue, at 102:1 it has no bodily seat under affliction, and at 107:5 it drains the wanderers' soul from hunger. Here the spirit is the seat and grief the weight.

Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be agitated / disquieted. Target (107) 'none'. Manner (108) is present: 'so much that speech fails' — the agitation so severe it leaves him mute. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the trouble with the sleepless eyes God holds open — the disturbance welded to enforced wakefulness. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the agitation that robs even words; paam here the inner disturbance so severe it leaves the sufferer mute, grief past the reach of speech. The inner-being process: an interior shaken past the point of language, held awake and speechless by its own turmoil.
narratives.story: The psalmist is so shaken inside that he cannot even speak — his grief has gone past the reach of words. God holds his eyes open through the night, and in that forced wakefulness his whole self churns and trembles. The disturbance isn't lodged in one part of him; it unsettles the entire person. It is turmoil so deep that language fails and he is left awake and silent.

Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; a whole-self (and whole-people) abasement. Bearer (105) is 'we', the people — a corporate sufferer, not an individual. Operation (106) to be brought very low. Target (107) is 'under judgment' — the low estate read as the condition of a people beneath God's chastening. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the abasement with the confessed iniquities — the being-brought-low bound to acknowledged sin. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the abasement of the people, reduced and weakened, the low estate that grounds the appeal for speedy compassion. The inner-being process: a people reduced and weakened under judgment, making their very lowness the ground of their plea for mercy.
narratives.story: A whole people confesses that they have been brought very low — reduced, weakened, beneath God's judgment. They set this lowness against their own past sins, owning the connection. It isn't the state of one person but of the community, and it isn't fixed in the body; it is the whole people humbled. And they turn that very lowness into a reason for God to send his compassion quickly.

Operation (106) is to suffer oppression; target (107) is 'under injustice' — the affliction read as the fruit of failed justice. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the afflicted with the destitute — the poor and needy together. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the humbled poor, their affliction the measure of the judges' failure. The inner-being process: affliction here is the standing condition of a whole class of the oppressed, whose suffering under injustice is the very yardstick by which the unjust rulers are judged.
narratives.story: God confronts unjust judges and points to the afflicted — the humbled poor, the destitute and needy — whose suffering the judges have ignored. Here 'afflicted' names not one man's pain but a whole class of oppressed people, ground down under injustice. Their affliction is not incidental; it is the measure of how badly the powerful have failed. Their low condition becomes the standard by which the judges themselves are weighed.
narratives.variation_note: This afflict reading differs from the item's others by its bearer: not the psalmist but 'the afflicted' as a social class — the oppressed poor. Unlike the personal loneliness of 25:16, the pain-and-rescue of 69:29, the lifelong affliction of 88:15, or the prayer-from-affliction of 102:1, at 82:3 the affliction is corporate and public, the yardstick of unjust judges' guilt.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be dismayed (bahal, Psa 83:17). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the enemies — the descent read at full weight: this is dismay invoked upon the hostile foe, not suffered by the psalmist. Operation (106) to be dismayed / terrified; target (107) is 'under judgment' — the terror as the condition of the judged foe. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the dismay with the shame — terror welded to disgrace. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the panic of the judged foe, terror answering their arrogance — and pointedly, this terror is asked for so 'that they may seek your name' (v16): dread aimed at turning the enemy to God. The inner-being process: a terror sought upon the enemy, their arrogance broken into panic, with the further hope that the dread will drive them to seek God.
narratives.story: The psalmist asks God to fill his enemies with terror and disgrace — to break their arrogance into panic under judgment. This is dread aimed at the foe, not felt by the psalmist himself. It comes joined to shame, the two together undoing them. And there is a further edge to it: the terror is asked for so that, shattered, the enemies might finally seek God's name. The panic is meant to bend them back toward him.
narratives.variation_note: This dismay differs from the item's others by bearer: here it is invoked on the enemies (a descent read), whereas at 30:7 it strikes the psalmist himself when God hides his face, and at 90:7 it falls on all mortals before God's wrath. Uniquely here the terror carries a purpose — that the shattered foe might seek God — the same dread, but turned toward the enemy's conversion.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): faint (kalah, 'yes, faints for the courts of the LORD', Psa 84:2). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located, though the verse names soul, heart and flesh together. Bearer (105) is the pilgrim — not distress but a worshipper longing for the temple. Operation (106) to faint / be spent; target (107) is 'with longing' — the key distinctive: this fainting is the swoon of desire, the self spent in yearning for God's courts. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the fainting with the longing soul — the collapse welded to yearning, not to despair. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the swooning of desire, the self spent in yearning for God. The inner-being process: longing so intense the self is spent by it — exhaustion born of love for God's dwelling, weakness that is a form of worship.
narratives.story: The pilgrim's whole self longs for the temple so intensely that he faints for it — soul, heart, and body aching to be in God's courts. This is not the collapse of despair but the swoon of desire: he is spent by sheer yearning. His longing and his fainting are one and the same movement. The weakness here is really a kind of worship — wanting God so much it wears him out.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): grow dim (daab, 'my eye grows dim through sorrow', Psa 88:9). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, though target names sorrow as the wearing cause. Seat (104) 'none' as a formal slot, yet the reading fixes on the eye — grief worn into the body's very sight. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to have the eye grow dim; target (107) is 'through sorrow' — the dimming caused by prolonged grief. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the dimming with the sorrow. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the wasting of the very sight, grief worn into the body. The inner-being process: sorrow so sustained it wears down the physical faculty of sight — the interior grief registering as the eye failing, the self visibly wasting in a psalm that finds no relief.
narratives.story: The psalmist's eyes are failing, worn dim by unending sorrow. His grief has gone on so long that it shows in his body — his very sight is wearing out. This comes in one of the darkest of all the psalms, where no rescue arrives. Nothing softens it: the sorrow simply grinds him down until even his eyes give way.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): suffer (nasa, 'I suffer your terrors', Psa 88:15). Type (102) is 'action' — the self actively bears the terror, not merely undergoes a status. Source (103) absent as a slot, though the terrors are God's. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to bear / suffer; target (107) is 'God's terrors' — the dread the self carries is God-sent. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the suffering with helplessness — 'I suffer your terrors; I am helpless': the bearing welded to a total inability to escape. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the bearing of God-sent dread, terror endured to the point of collapse. The inner-being process: the self carrying a dread it attributes to God himself, and carrying it to the edge of helplessness — an active enduring that nonetheless ends in powerlessness.
narratives.story: The psalmist says he carries God's own terrors — he bears them, and it leaves him helpless. This is not just a state that happens to him; he is actively holding up under a dread he traces to God, and the weight of it empties him of any power to escape. Afflicted and near death since his youth, he suffers this terror to the very edge of collapse. The bearing and the helplessness are one: he endures, yet can do nothing.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): afflicted (ani, 'Afflicted... from my youth up', Psa 88:15). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be afflicted; target (107) is 'from youth' — the distinctive here is duration: affliction spanning a whole life. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the affliction with suffering and helplessness — lifelong affliction welded to the bearing of terror and to powerlessness. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): a lifetime of suffering, affliction as the sufferer's whole history. The inner-being process: affliction not as a passing episode but as the entire biography of the self — close to death from youth up, a life defined by it, with no relief in view.
narratives.story: The psalmist says he has been afflicted and close to death since he was young — his whole life has been shaped by suffering. This is not one bad season but his entire story. It joins his bearing of terror and his helplessness into a single, lifelong condition. And in this bleakest of psalms, nothing lifts it; affliction is simply the whole history of who he has been.
narratives.variation_note: This afflict reading differs from the item's others by its span: a whole lifetime, 'from youth up'. Unlike the lonely affliction of 25:16, the pain-and-rescue turn of 69:29, the oppressed-class of 82:3, or the prayer-from-affliction of 102:1, at 88:15 affliction is the sufferer's entire biography — lifelong, welded to helplessness, with no relief in view.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be dismayed (bahal, 'by your wrath we are dismayed', Psa 90:7). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, though target names God's wrath. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) is 'we', mankind — the widest bearer of this word in the family: not the psalmist alone nor the enemy, but all mortals. Operation (106) to be terrified / dismayed; target (107) is 'by God's wrath' — the dread of humankind before divine anger. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs the dismay with being consumed — terror welded to the mortality that sweeps humans away like grass. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal ib-state. Discovery (114): the terror of mortals before God's anger, dread at their own frailty. The inner-being process: humankind as such trembling before God's wrath, the dismay bound up with the awareness of being consumed — dread that is really the interior of human mortality.
narratives.story: Here it is not one person or one enemy but all people who are dismayed — terrified before God's anger. The dread is bound up with being swept away: humans are like grass that flourishes in the morning and fades by evening, and this terror is the inner face of that frailty. It grips the whole self, not any one part. It is the dread of mortals who feel how easily they are consumed.
narratives.variation_note: This dismay is the item's widest reading by bearer: all mankind, not the psalmist (as at 30:7) nor the enemies (as at 83:17). At 90:7 the terror is the universal dread of mortals before God's wrath, welded to the awareness of being consumed — a dismay that is really the interior of human mortality itself.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): afflict (anah, 'and afflict your heritage', Psa 94:5). Type (102) is 'action' — distinctively active: affliction here is inflicted, not suffered. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none'. Bearer (105) is the wicked — the doer of affliction, read at full weight: this is the aggressor's interior in motion. Operation (106) to afflict; target (107) is 'God's heritage' — the wicked's affliction aimed at God's people. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) pairs it with crushing the people. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) is given as 'paired with crushing the people' — the affliction bound to the act of crushing. Discovery (114): the tormenting of God's inheritance by the wicked. The inner-being process: affliction as the wicked's own outgoing act — the aggressor crushing and afflicting God's people, the dark interior expressed as harm done to others.
narratives.story: This time affliction is something done, not suffered: the wicked crush God's people and afflict his heritage. The word names the aggressor in action — the arrogant and the evildoers grinding down the widow, the stranger, the fatherless. Their affliction of others is bound up with crushing them. Read honestly, this is the dark face of the same word: an interior that expresses itself by inflicting suffering on the helpless.
narratives.variation_note: This afflict reading is the item's aggressor-reading: the bearer is the wicked and the type is active (they afflict others), unlike 35:13 where the psalmist afflicts himself in compassion, and unlike 116:10, 119:67 and 119:107 where the psalmist bears affliction received. Same root, opposite pole — here affliction is harm inflicted on God's people, the descent read as fully as the ascent.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): faint (ataph, 'when he is faint and pours out his complaint', Psa 102:1 superscription). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located — unlike 61:2 (heart) and 77:3 (spirit), here the fainting has no bodily seat. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to grow faint; target (107) is 'under affliction' — the fainting is the weakness of the afflicted one. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) is 'internal:ib-state' — the fainting held as an inner condition. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with being afflicted' — the reading welds the faintness to the affliction it accompanies. Discovery (114): the swooning weakness from which the lament pours. The inner-being process: an afflicted self grown so faint that its very prayer is a pouring-out from weakness — the lament rising precisely out of the swoon.
narratives.story: The heading of this psalm calls it the prayer of an afflicted man who is faint and pours out his complaint before God. His fainting isn't tied to any part of the body — it is simply the weakness of a self worn down by affliction. And out of that weakness the whole prayer comes: the lament is what the faintness pours out. He is spent, and the spending itself becomes his cry to God.
narratives.variation_note: This fainting differs from the item's others by having no bodily seat: at 102:1 it is unlocated (contrast the heart at 61:2 and the spirit at 77:3), and it is welded specifically to affliction, the swoon from which the lament pours. Unlike the wanderers' hunger-faint at 107:5, here it is the individual afflicted self, faint and praying.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): afflicted (ani, 'A prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint', Psa 102:1). Type (102) 'status'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be afflicted; target (107) is 'before God' — the affliction is one held out in prayer. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with being faint' — the affliction welded to the faintness of the same verse. Discovery (114): the sufferer whose whole prayer rises from affliction. The inner-being process: affliction here is the defining identity of the one praying — not an episode but the very standpoint from which the prayer is offered, the afflicted self pouring itself out before God.
narratives.story: This psalm is headed 'a prayer of one afflicted' — the word names not just what he feels but who he is as he prays. His affliction and his faintness go together, and the whole prayer rises out of them. He is defined by his suffering here, and it is from that place, laid open before God, that he speaks. The affliction is the very ground he prays from.
narratives.variation_note: This afflict reading is marked by identity: at 102:1 'afflicted' is the standpoint of the one praying — the prayer rises from affliction and is welded to faintness. Unlike the lonely affliction of 25:16, the pain-and-rescue of 69:29, the oppressed class of 82:3, or the lifelong affliction of 88:15, here affliction names who the pray-er is as he pours himself out before God.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): withered (yabesh, 'My heart is struck down like grass and has withered', Psa 102:4). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none' as a formal slot, but target and locus fix it in the heart — the drying-up is of the heart itself. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to be withered; target (107) is 'in heart' — the vitality of the heart dried out. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with the struck-down heart'. Discovery (114): the drying-up of the heart, vitality gone in the affliction. The inner-being process: the heart, struck down like mown grass, drying out - life-sap withdrawn from the very seat of the self, so that even eating is forgotten.
narratives.story: The psalmist says his heart has been struck down like grass and has dried up. The living sap has gone out of him — the very centre of the self shrivelled, so that he even forgets to eat. It is the picture of a heart cut down and left to wither in the sun. His vitality has simply drained away under his affliction.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): wither away (yabesh, 'I wither away like grass', Psa 102:11). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, though the passage traces it to God's indignation ('you have taken me up and thrown me down'). Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the whole self fades. Bearer (105) the psalmist; operation (106) to wither away; target (107) is 'like grass' — the self fading as cut grass fades. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with the evening-shadow days'. Discovery (114): the fading of the sufferer, life drying up like cut grass. The inner-being process: the whole self fading like an evening shadow and drying like grass — a life visibly ebbing away, felt as God's having lifted him up only to cast him down.
narratives.story: The psalmist feels his life fading like an evening shadow and drying up like cut grass. This time it is not just his heart but his whole self wasting away. He traces it to God's anger — as if he had been picked up and thrown down. Day by day he simply withers, life ebbing out of him like grass losing its green.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): be hurt (anah, 'His feet were hurt with fetters', Psa 105:18). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot. Seat (104) 'none' as a formal slot, though the target names the feet in irons. Bearer (105) is Joseph — not the psalmist but a remembered figure, his affliction recalled from Israel's history. Operation (106) to be afflicted; target (107) is 'his feet hurt with fetters' — the affliction registered as bodily bondage. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with his exaltation to bind princes at his pleasure' — the affliction set against the later exaltation. Discovery (114): Joseph's affliction in the pit of slavery, the low point before the exaltation. The inner-being process: affliction as a remembered low — Joseph bound and hurt in slavery, a suffering the psalm holds up precisely as the dark point from which God later lifted him to rule.
narratives.story: The psalm recalls Joseph, whose feet were hurt with fetters and whose neck was put in iron — the bondage of his slavery. This is affliction remembered from Israel's story, not the psalmist's own. And it is deliberately set against what came later: the same Joseph, once bound, was raised up to rule. The suffering is held up as the low point out of which God brought him high.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): affliction (oni, 'prisoners in affliction and in irons', Psa 107:10). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, but the coupling names it: they had rebelled against God. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the prisoners — a group of sufferers, one of the psalm's typical plights. Operation (106) to sit in affliction; target (107) is 'and irons' — affliction as bound imprisonment. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with rebelling against God'. Discovery (114): the bound and suffering, the second plight. The inner-being process: affliction here is a self-incurred bondage — those who spurned God's counsel sit in darkness and irons, their affliction bound to their own rebellion, until they cry out and are delivered.
narratives.story: Some sit in darkness, prisoners in misery and chains — and the psalm says it came because they had rebelled against God and spurned his counsel. Their affliction is a bondage they brought on themselves. It grips the whole person, not one part. Yet the story does not end there: when they cry out in their trouble, God delivers them. The misery is real, and so is the rescue that follows.
narratives.variation_note: This affliction differs from the item's others by bearer and cause: at 107:10 it is a group of prisoners, and it is self-incurred — bound to their rebellion against God. Unlike the individual plea of 9:13, the nation's unrelieved affliction of 44:24, or the promise-sustained affliction of 119:50, here affliction is a company's chains, consequence of their own spurning of God, from which they are later delivered.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): faint (ataph, 'their soul fainted within them', Psa 107:5). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, though target names hunger and thirst. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the soul faints as a whole. Bearer (105) is the wanderers — a group, not the psalmist: those lost in desert wastes. Operation (106) to faint / grow feeble; target (107) is 'from hunger and thirst' — the fainting caused by physical want. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with the soul'. Discovery (114): the swooning of the wanderers, life ebbing in the waste. The inner-being process: the soul fainting under bodily deprivation — hunger and thirst draining the inner self of life in a trackless waste, until they cry out and are led to a city.
narratives.story: Some wander lost in the desert, hungry and thirsty, and their soul faints away inside them. Here the collapse comes from plain physical want — no food, no water, no way to a city. It isn't fixed in one part of them; the whole inner self ebbs. Then they cry out to God in their trouble, and he leads them by a straight road to a place to live. The fainting is real, but so is the deliverance.
narratives.variation_note: This fainting differs from the item's others by bearer and cause: at 107:5 it is a group of wanderers, and it is driven by hunger and thirst — physical deprivation. Unlike the heart-faint of 61:2, the spirit-faint under grief at 77:3, or the affliction-faint of 102:1, here the soul faints from bodily want in the wilderness, answered by God's leading.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): suffered affliction (anah, 'because of their iniquities suffered affliction', Psa 107:17). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, but coupling names the cause: their iniquities. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located. Bearer (105) is 'the fools' — those whose sinful ways brought this on them. Operation (106) to suffer affliction; target (107) is 'for their sin' — affliction as the consequence of sin. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with the iniquities'. Discovery (114): the sickness endured as sin's consequence — they loathed food and drew near the gates of death. The inner-being process: affliction as the fruit of one's own folly — the sick self, brought low by its sins to the very edge of death, from which the cry to God brings healing.
narratives.story: Some were fools who went their own sinful way, and because of it they suffered — sick, unable to eat, drawn close to death's door. Their affliction is the fruit of their own folly. Yet again the psalm turns: when they cry to God in their trouble, he sends his word and heals them. The suffering is owned as sin's consequence, and the rescue comes all the same.

narratives.narrative: Sense (101): melt (mug, 'their courage melted away', Psa 107:26). Type (102) 'state'. Source (103) absent as a slot, though the storm is the trigger. Seat (104) 'none': not organ-located; the courage — the inner nerve — dissolves. Bearer (105) is the sailors — a group at sea, not the psalmist. Operation (106) to have courage melt away; target (107) is 'in terror' — the melting caused by the storm's dread. Manner (108) 'none'; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. Coupling (112) 'internal:ib-state'. Prohibition (113) absent. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) 'paired with the courage'. Discovery (114): the dissolving of the sailors' nerve before the storm. The inner-being process: courage — the inner steadiness of the self — liquefying under terror; as the ship heaves up to heaven and down to the depths, their nerve dissolves and they reel like drunken men, until they cry to God and are stilled.
narratives.story: Caught in a violent storm at sea, the sailors' courage simply melts away inside them. As the waves throw the ship up to the sky and down to the depths, their nerve dissolves and they stagger about like drunk men, at their wits' end. The steadiness that held them gives way to terror. Then they cry to God, and he hushes the storm to a whisper. The collapse of nerve is real, and so is the calm that answers it.

narratives.story: The psalm asks God to remember all the hardships David endured — the self-denial he took on for the sake of building God a house. This is affliction chosen, not merely suffered: David wore himself out with a single purpose, bound to the vow he swore to the Mighty One of Jacob. The hardship is the very shape of his devotion. He gave himself no rest until God had a dwelling place, and the psalm holds that costly commitment up to be remembered.
